scenes.title:
Patterns are built on
**eight structures**.
scenes.sub: What each one is for, and what each step costs.
say: Two pointers, sliding window, B F S, dynamic programming.

say.say: Most patterns you'll meet are built on the same eight structures.
In this video: what each one is for, and what each step costs.

scenes.label: 1 · ARRAY
scenes.title: A row of boxes, each with an index
say: An array is a row of boxes, side by side. Each box has a number, called its index, starting from zero.

say.say: Ask for a at index 2, and you get {{A2}}, straight away. Reading by index costs O of 1.
say.show: Ask for a[2], and you get {{A2}}, straight away. Reading by index costs O(1).

say.say: Its length is {{LEN}}. Searching for a value, though, means walking the whole row.

scenes.label: 2 · STRING
scenes.title: A row of characters
say: A string is the same idea: a row of characters, read by index. The box at index 0 holds c.

say.say: Taking a substring copies characters, so it costs O of n. From index 1, you get o, d, e.

scenes.label: 3 · HASH MAP
scenes.title: Key in, value out
head: PSEUDOCODE
WHAT HAPPENS
say: A hash map stores pairs: a key, and its value. Store apple with the value 3.

say.say: Give it the key apple, and it hands back 3, on average in O of 1.
say.show: Give it the key apple, and it hands back 3, on average in O(1).

say: Ask whether fig is in it, and the answer is false.

scenes.label: 4 · HASH SET
scenes.title: Have I seen this before?
say: A hash set is a bag of unique values. Add 9.

say.say: Add 9 again, and nothing changes. It keeps one copy.
It answers one question, fast. Have I seen this value? Is 4 in it? No.

scenes.label: 5 · STACK
scenes.title: Last in, first out

states.note: `top of st` is **{{TOP}}**, only a look

say.say: A stack is a pile of plates. You only touch the top one. Push 5 onto a stack holding 3.

say: Look at the top, and you see 5, without removing it.

say.say: Pop, and 5 comes off. The top is 3 again. Each of these is O of 1.

scenes.label: 6 · QUEUE
scenes.title: First in, first out

states.note: `add 8 to q`: joins at the back

say: A queue is a ticket line. You join at the back. Add 8 behind 4.

say.say: You leave from the front. Remove the front, and you get 4, the one that came first.

say: Now 8 is at the front. Breadth-first search runs on this.

scenes.label: 7 · LINKED LIST
scenes.title: Each node knows only the next
say: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value, and a pointer to the next node.

say.say: To reach the third node, you walk from the head, one step at a time. So reaching node k costs O of k.

scenes.label: 8 · BINARY TREE
scenes.title: Up to two children each
say: A binary tree starts at the root. Every node has up to two children, a left and a right.

say.say: The root holds 8. Its left child holds 3, and its right child holds 10. A node with no children is a leaf.

scenes.label: THE COST
scenes.title: What each step costs
head: STRUCTURE
STEP
COST

say.say: Here's the whole picture. Reading by index is instant. Searching a row means looking at every box.

say: Maps and sets add and find in constant time, on average.
Stacks and queues work only at their ends, so every step is constant.
Lists and trees are walked one node at a time.

note.text: The last box is `a[length(a) - 1]`. `a[length(a)]` is past the end.

say.say: Here's a mistake beginners make. They read a at index 2 as the second box, and expect 2.
say.show: Here's a mistake beginners make. They read a[2] as the second box, and expect 2.

say.say: But counting starts at zero, so index 2 is the third box. The answer is 9.
So the last box is at length minus 1. Ask for index length, and you've gone past the end.
say.show: So the last box is a[length(a) - 1]. a[length(a)] is past the end.

short.title: a[2] is not the second box

say.say: Quick one. In this array, what is a at index 2?
say.show: Quick one. In this array, what is a[2]?

say.say: If you said 2, the second box, you've hit the trap.

scenes.label: INDEXES START AT 0
scenes.title: Count from **zero**
say: Indexes start at zero. The first box is index 0, the second is index 1.

say.say: So index 2 is the third box. The answer is 9.
Same trap at the other end. The last box is at length minus 1, which is 4.
say.show: Same trap at the other end. The last box is a[length(a) - 1], index 4.

say.say: Index 5 doesn't exist. That's the out of bounds error.
say.show: Index 5 doesn't exist. That's the index-out-of-bounds error.
